did_you_know.text: In Biblical Hebrew, the word “language” can also mean “lip,” the organ of speech. The verse therefore points not only to one language, but also to shared communication.
“The land of Shinar” is generally understood as southern Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers, where ancient cities such as Babylon developed.

Stone was scarce in southern Mesopotamia, so mud bricks and fired bricks were important building materials. The “mortar” in the verse is commonly identified as bitumen, a natural asphalt-like substance used as binding material.

Stepped towers called ziggurats were prominent in Mesopotamian cities and served as religious centers. The tower in the story may recall such buildings, although the Bible does not identify it explicitly as a ziggurat.

The story presents different languages as making cooperation difficult, but it does not say which languages appeared or how. Scientifically, languages change and split gradually over many generations.
The name “Babel” is linked here by a wordplay to the Hebrew root meaning “to mix” or “confuse.” In Akkadian, however, Babylon’s name is connected with a phrase meaning “gate of the god.”

In the genealogy from Shem to Terah, the listed lifespans generally become shorter, although the number does not decrease in every generation. The list creates a bridge from the post-Flood world to Abraham’s family.
The name “Peleg” is related to the Hebrew root meaning “to divide” or “split.” Genesis 10:25 explains his name by saying that in his days “the earth was divided.”

“Ur of the Chaldeans” is often identified with the ancient city of Ur in modern southern Iraq, but the identification is not completely certain. The question remains debated because the term “Chaldeans” became common especially in later periods.

In the ancient world, children were often seen as the continuation of a family and as economic support, so infertility brought social as well as personal hardship. The Bible describes Sarai’s situation without blaming her.

Haran was an important city in northern Mesopotamia, in the region of modern Turkey, and lay on trade routes linking Mesopotamia, Syria, and Canaan. It was therefore a natural stopping place for a family traveling west.
